title: New Study Says Rosalind Franklin Knew Her Famous DNA Photo Was Important
summary:
DNA is the molecule that carries the instructions for every living thing. In 1962, three scientists, Francis Crick, James Watson and Maurice Wilkins, won a Nobel Prize for discovering that DNA is shaped like a double helix, a twisted ladder. But their work depended on X-ray photographs taken by another scientist, Rosalind Franklin.

A new study suggests Franklin understood more than she was given credit for. Historian Alistair Sponsel of the Science History Institute in Philadelphia and scientist Brian Sutton of King's College London studied her notes and photos. Their work was published Monday in the Journal of the History of Biology.

Franklin's most famous image is called Photograph 51, taken in May 1952. Some stories said it was an experimental shot she thought was unimportant. Watson also suggested she was good at taking pictures but bad at understanding them.

The new research tells a different story. Franklin first photographed the DNA sample in Photograph 49, and her notes for that picture mention a possible helical shape. The same day she saw it, she started a new, sharper photo of the same sample: Photograph 51.

"She took it because she wanted to get a really refined version," Sponsel told Live Science. That effort, he said, is "a sign she knew she had something really important on her hands."

The researchers say Franklin chose to study another form of DNA first because it seemed to hold more data. During that time, Wilkins showed Watson her photographs. Watson and Crick then built their double helix model.

Franklin died in 1958, which made her ineligible for the later prize. Live Science notes the study suggests she found DNA's helical shape, not the full double helix.
why_it_matters: The study changes how people remember who contributed to one of the biggest discoveries in biology. It shows that credit in science can depend on how stories are told, and that careful historical research can correct them.

background_read: DNA is the molecule inside cells that carries the instructions for how living things grow and work.
X-ray crystallography is a method in which scientists shine X-rays at a sample and study the patterns the rays make to figure out the shape of molecules.
Knowing DNA's twisted-ladder shape helped scientists understand how genetic information is copied and passed on.
Historians of science study old notebooks, letters and photographs to learn who made a discovery and how it happened.
